extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, peer-review researchers, and biomedical journal policy‑makers
extracted.subtask_description: Systematic review/meta-analysis criteria and outcomes used to evaluate interventions aimed at improving the quality, speed, and decisions of peer review in biomedical journals. Focuses on randomized controlled trials of interventions (training, statistical reviewers, checklists, open/blinded review, process changes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Final manuscript quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Final manuscript quality (i.e., revised manuscript after all peer review assessments and rounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured using several scales (e.g., the Manuscript Quality Assessment Instrument, a 34‑item scale) and scales based on reporting guideline items (e.g., CONSORT items). A high score indicates a high quality manuscript. Different scales exist across trials; when pooling, standardized mean differences (SMDs) are used because instruments vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of the peer review report
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of the peer review report, measured by scales such as the Review Quality Instrument (RQI) or editor routine quality rating scales. A high score indicates a high quality peer review report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RQI (latest version) is based on eight items: importance, originality, methodology, presentation, constructiveness of comments, substantiation of comments and interpretation of results, plus a global item; each item scored 1–5. RQI has shown inter-rater reliability measures (e.g., K = 0.83 agreement for total score; K = 0.31 inter-rater reliability in mean total score). Use SMD when combining different review quality scales across studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejection rate: recommendation by peer reviewers about whether or not the reviewed manuscripts should be rejected from publication in the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured as a dichotomous outcome (number of manuscripts for which reviewers recommended rejection vs. total manuscripts evaluated). Pooled effect sizes reported as odds ratios (ORs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time spent on the peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Time spent on the peer review as reported by peer reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported in minutes/hours per review; important to evaluate burden and possible cost of peer review. When analyzed across studies with different measures, mean differences or SMDs may be used. Time‑spent outcome was added post‑hoc in this review when studies were found reporting it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall duration of the peer review process
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall duration of the peer review process (e.g., time to manuscript decision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured as time from submission to editorial decision or other workflow timepoints. Used to evaluate interventions intended to accelerate peer review. Outcomes sometimes incompletely reported and heterogeneous across trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training (intervention category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Training, which included training or mentoring programs for peer reviewers to provide instructional support for appropriately evaluating important components of manuscript submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interventions include structured workshops with editors, self‑taught training packages, mentoring (new reviewers discuss reviews with senior reviewers), and feedback (copy of editor’s rating given to reviewer). In the included RCTs, training had no clear impact on review quality; heterogeneity across studies was high and many trials had high attrition bias. Training effects on time and rejection rate were inconsistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition of a statistical peer reviewer (intervention category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Addition of peer reviewers for specific tasks or with specific expertise such as adding a statistical peer reviewer, whose main task is to detect the misuse of methods or misreporting of statistical analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessed as adding a dedicated statistical reviewer to the peer review process. In the trials (Medicina Clínica), adding a statistical peer reviewer improved the quality of the final manuscript (combined SMD 0.58; 95% CI 0.19–0.98). Evidence came from a small number of trials in a single journal and needs replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer reviewers’ use of a checklist (intervention category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers’ use of a checklist, such as reporting guideline checklists, to evaluate the quality of the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checklists refer to reporting‑guideline based instruments (e.g., CONSORT items). Two RCTs evaluated this and overall found no effect on the quality of the final manuscript (combined SMD 0.19; 95% CI –0.22 to 0.61). Studies were conducted in the same journal/group; consider contextual factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open peer review (intervention category)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Open” peer review process, whereby peer reviewers are informed that their name would be revealed to the authors, other peer reviewers, and/or the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Types of openness evaluated: identity revealed to other peer reviewers, to authors, and publicly posted (web). Open peer review increased the quality of peer review reports (combined SMD 0.14; 95% CI 0.05–0.24), decreased recommendation to reject (OR 0.56; 95% CI 0.33–0.94), and had no clear effect on time spent. Subgroup analyses by intensity of openness (open to other reviewers vs. to authors vs. public) did not show strong differences. Heterogeneity for rejection rate was substantial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinded/masked peer review (intervention category)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Blinded”/masked peer review, whereby peer reviewers are blinded to author names and affiliation (author identifiers removed from manuscripts sent for review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blinded review intended to reduce bias from knowing author identity. In pooled RCTs, blinding did not affect quality of peer review reports (SMD 0.12; 95% CI –0.12 to 0.36) or rejection rate (OR 0.77; 95% CI 0.39 to 1.50), with substantial heterogeneity and wide CIs. Different masking approaches and study designs contribute to heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interventions to accelerate the peer review process
rubrics_metrics.description: Other interventions intended to increase the speed of the peer review process (e.g., early editorial screening, asking referees if they agree to review before sending manuscript, calling referees first).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outcomes include time to decision and overall duration. One trial reported decreased duration with early editorial screening; other RCTs had incomplete reporting and heterogeneity prevented meta-analysis. Consider both effectiveness and potential tradeoffs with quality and reviewer burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript Quality Assessment Instrument (MQAI)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Manuscript Quality Assessment Instrument (MQAI): a 34‑item scale, each item scored from 1 to 5, aimed to evaluate the quality of the research report (i.e., whether the authors have described their research in enough detail and clarity to allow independent judgment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MQAI is organized along article sections (Title and Abstract, Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, Conclusions, and General evaluation). Used as an outcome measure in trials assessing final manuscript quality; higher scores indicate better reporting quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review Quality Instrument (RQI)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Review Quality Instrument (RQI) is an instrument for assessing peer review reports; the last version is based on eight items each scored 1–5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items include importance, originality, methodology, presentation, constructiveness, substantiation of comments and interpretation, plus a global item. The RQI has demonstrated acceptable agreement and inter‑rater reliability in studies; different versions exist and trials used different RQI versions (v3.2, v4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cochrane risk of bias domains for RCTs (selection, detection, attrition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of risk of bias within each RCT used Cochrane Collaboration tool domains: selection bias (random sequence generation and allocation concealment), detection bias (blinding of outcome assessors), and attrition bias (incomplete outcome data). Performance bias (blinding of participants/providers) was not assessed because blinding was generally impossible in this context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each domain rated low, high or unclear risk. Blinding of outcome assessors and incomplete outcome data domains are assessed at the outcome level. When unclear, contact authors for information. If peer reviewers were unaware of the study hypothesis or outcome assessed, detection bias could be rated low.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of randomization (methodological criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unit of randomization used in trials: peer reviewers, manuscripts, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of unit affects study design, analysis, and interpretation (e.g., clustering, sample size). Trials in this review randomized peer reviewers (n=15), manuscripts (n=6) or both (n=4); report unit clearly and account for it in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre‑specification of outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcomes specified a priori for the trials/systematic review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All outcomes were pre‑specified in the review except 'time spent on the peer review', which was added after inspection of included studies. Pre‑specification reduces selective outcome reporting bias; when multiple measures exist, select primary outcome or latest timepoint per Cochrane guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence synthesis and heterogeneity assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Meta-analytic methods and heterogeneity assessment used to pool trial results (use of SMDs for continuous outcomes with different scales; ORs for binary outcomes; random‑effects meta‑analysis due to diversity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Dersimonian and Laird random‑effects model when interventions/settings are diverse. Assess heterogeneity with forest plots, Cochrane’s Q test and I2 statistic. Perform subgroup analyses (e.g., intensity/type of open peer review) when appropriate. For continuous outcomes mixing change and final values, avoid combining them as SMDs per Cochrane recommendations.
